Professional Practice III
Patient safety & Infection control
Invasive procedures

Quick Overview

This lesson covers asepsis and how it is applied during invasive procedures and surgery. It distinguishes medical (clean) asepsis from surgical (sterile) asepsis, which is divided into aseptic technique and sterile technique. It then explains safe surgery: the main causes of adverse events, the operating room environment and staff requirements, and the measures taken before, during and after an operation. It ends with a note on choosing and handling multidose versus single-dose vials.

Asepsis

Asepsis is a condition in which no living disease-causing microorganisms are present. It covers all procedures designed to reduce the risk of bacterial, fungal or viral contamination.

Asepsis is either medical or surgical. Surgical (sterile) asepsis includes procedures that eliminate or decrease the number of microorganisms to a level not harmful to health during invasive procedures, and it takes the form of either aseptic technique or sterile technique.

TypePurpose / when usedExamples
Medical (clean) asepsis Reduces the number of organisms and prevents their spread. Taking blood pressures, examining patients, feeding patients.
Aseptic technique (surgical asepsis) Brief invasive procedures that may break the skin or mucous membranes, or enter normally sterile parts of the body. Placement of IV lines and indwelling urinary catheters; wound care; preparation and administration of IV fluids; IV and IM injections, especially from multidose vials.
Sterile (surgical) technique (surgical asepsis) Surgery and invasive procedures with high rates of infection. Any long invasive procedure; placement of central lines and thoracic lines.

Safe Surgery

Causes of adverse events

The three main causes of adverse events in surgical care are:

  • Poor infection control methods.
  • Inadequate patient management.
  • Failure of effective communication.

Phases of a surgical procedure

Surgical procedures are divided into three phases: preoperative, intraoperative and postoperative. Both the operating room environment and the operating room staff must be taken into consideration.

Operating room environment and staff

Environment

  • Airborne bacteria must be minimized.
  • Surfaces must be kept clean.

Staff

  • Hand disinfection: surgical hand disinfection should be performed by all persons participating in the operative procedure.
  • Attire: all persons in the theatre wear surgical attire that is restricted to the surgical area; sterile gloves are used and no jewelry is worn.
  • A surgical mask is worn by everyone entering the operating room, and sterile surgical gowns must be worn.

Preoperative phase

  • Patient preparation: bathing, hair clipping and a sterile drape.
  • Antimicrobial prophylaxis: given within 1 hour before the incision and discontinued within 24 hours after surgery.

Intraoperative phase

This phase involves skin preparation, a sterile field with drapes, and the surgical technique itself.

  • Skin preparation: povidone iodine (7.5–10%) applied in a circular motion.
  • Sterile field: the sterile field must be maintained.
  • Surgical technique: aseptic technique with minimum tissue trauma; removal of dead tissue and foreign bodies; maintenance of adequate blood and oxygen supply; control of bleeding to prevent hematoma.

Postoperative phase

  • Wound dressing in the surgical ward: use aseptic technique, and do not open the dressing for 48 hours after the operation.
  • Postoperative stay: keep it as short as possible.

Safe injection practice rules also apply and are covered in the next chapter.

Multidose vs. Single-use Vials

A multidose vial is a vial of liquid medication intended for parenteral administration (injection or infusion) that contains more than one dose. If possible, choose a single-dose vial.

If a multidose vial must be used:

Keep one multidose vial for each patient and store it with the patient's name on it in a separate treatment or medication room. Wipe the access diaphragm (septum) with 70% alcohol.

Key Points / Quick Review

Asepsis

  • No living disease-causing microorganisms present.
  • Medical (clean): reduces and prevents spread of organisms (e.g. blood pressure, examining, feeding).
  • Surgical: aseptic technique or sterile technique.

Aseptic vs. Sterile Technique

  • Aseptic: brief invasive procedures (IV lines, urinary catheters, wound care, IV fluids, IV/IM injections).
  • Sterile: surgery and long or high-infection-risk procedures (central and thoracic lines).

Adverse Events

  • Poor infection control, inadequate patient management, failure of communication.

Operating Room

  • Minimize airborne bacteria; keep surfaces clean.
  • Surgical hand disinfection for all participants; attire restricted to the surgical area; sterile gloves, no jewelry; masks for everyone; sterile gowns.

Pre- and Intraoperative

  • Pre-op: bathing, hair clipping, sterile drape; prophylaxis within 1 hour before incision, stopped within 24 hours after.
  • Intra-op: povidone iodine 7.5–10% in a circular motion; keep the field sterile; minimal tissue trauma; remove dead tissue and foreign bodies; maintain blood and oxygen supply; control bleeding.

Postoperative and Vials

  • Do not open the dressing for 48 hours; aseptic dressing; shortest possible stay.
  • Prefer single-dose vials; if multidose, one vial per patient, labeled and stored in a separate room, septum wiped with 70% alcohol.
